About

Customer Insight and CX Strategist. Banking, retail, education.

I help teams replace assumptions with observation. My work sits at the intersection of behavioural data, qualitative research and customer-experience design. I care less about which method we use than whether the answer holds up under scrutiny and ships into something real.

Over the past several years I have built behaviour-driven campaign engines for fintech, redesigned digital journeys for retail and education, diagnosed cultural friction blocking the adoption of a first-of-its-kind AI mall guide, and validated CX uplift with Cochran-grade statistical rigor. I write SQL, run interviews, build dashboards and present to leadership. I am just as comfortable removing an analytically valid insight that did not pass the trust test.

What I am best at: framing the right problem, choosing the cheapest method that will hold, communicating trade-offs clearly to stakeholders, and protecting customer trust even when it costs analytical sharpness.

How I work

A repeatable insight-to-action operating loop.

Every project I run goes through these four loops. The names change with context; the underlying loop does not.

STEP 01

Frame the problem

Replace the "increase X" brief with an observation-led diagnosis. Decide what kind of answer would actually move the decision.

STEP 02

Triangulate evidence

Combine behavioural data, qualitative research and CX signals. Pick the cheapest method that still holds up under scrutiny.

STEP 03

Translate into a decision

Write the insight in language stakeholders can act on. Surface the trade-offs and what will be true if we decide otherwise.

STEP 04

Measure and iterate

Define the metric that proves it: NPS, CSAT, conversion, churn. Validate statistically, watch for fatigue, course-correct quickly.

CX Field Research Operating System

Built and shipped solo · used by 50+ CX researchers across the bank

50+Active CX researchers
12Product tribes covered
3 minMax interview time
60 secTag-to-card latency

A real, shipped system. Open the live tool →

The problem

The bank had a fundamental scaling problem with field research. Customer Journey Experts (CJEs) across 12 product tribes were conducting interviews in branches, but every team had its own notebook, its own format, its own taxonomy. Insights got lost. The same question got asked four different ways. Nobody could see the full picture across products or branches. Aggregation was a manual nightmare, and by the time research reached leadership it was a month old.

What I built

A complete CX Field Research Operating System. One tool, used by every CX researcher in the bank, that standardises how field research is captured, tagged and aggregated. I designed and built it solo from A to Z: the methodology, the taxonomy, the branch workflow, the multi-user backend, the live dashboard.

What is in the system

  • Branch layout diagram showing exactly where each researcher sits relative to the 5 service windows, the queue kiosk and the customer waiting area. Removes ambiguity on day one.
  • 3-tag taxonomy applied to every interview: User Type (Active / Passive / Offline / Hybrid), Emotion (Confused / Frustrated / Neutral / Confident), CRM Exposure (Engaged / Dismissed / Unaware / Never Exposed). Designed to be tagged in under 60 seconds.
  • Methodology rules ("Do" and "Don't") baked into the tool so every CJE follows the same protocol: anchor on concrete time, no hypotheticals, no leading questions, no selling, 3-minute cap.
  • Worked example card showing exactly what a completed interview should look like, so new researchers have a reference within seconds of opening the tool.
  • Multi-user card creation: 50+ CJEs can create cards in parallel from their own browsers. Every card writes to a central Google Sheet via Apps Script. No login conflicts, no version mismatches.
  • Live dashboard that auto-aggregates every new card: KPI tiles, user-type distribution, emotion distribution, CRM exposure breakdown, branch-level performance, customer rating, friction themes, selected verbatims and an auto-generated insight summary.
  • 12 product-tribe filters: Kredit · Kartlar · Əmanət · Hesab Açma · ABB Play · Faydamania · Activation · Azal-Miles · Family · İpoteka · Hiper · Ümumi.
  • One-click export: CSV (for analysts) and JSON dashboard snapshot (for archival and external reporting).

Design decisions worth calling out

Why 3 minutes, not 10

Branch customers are mid-task. Their patience window for an interview is small. After 3 minutes, answer quality drops sharply and consent fatigue kicks in. Capping the protocol forces CJEs to ask only the questions that matter and ship the card before memory fades.

Why 3 tags, not 30

A taxonomy with 30 dimensions is intellectually satisfying and operationally dead. I deliberately compressed the framework to the smallest set that still discriminates: what kind of customer they are, how they feel, what they know about CRM touchpoints. Anything beyond that goes in the free-text fields, which feed the verbatim and friction-theme panels.

Why Google Sheets as the backend

I evaluated a "real" database but rejected it. Sheets is the operational lingua franca of every analyst in the bank. Apps Script as the API means: zero hosting cost, zero auth complexity for end users, instant CSV interoperability, and any non-technical CX lead can extend the schema without engineering tickets. The trade-off is rate limits, which I mitigate with retry-with-backoff and a sync-status indicator.

Why a customer rating field

Most field research collects observation, not customer voice on the experience itself. A 1-to-5 star rating from the customer at the end of every card gives us a calibration signal: when CJEs interpret a moment as "Confused" but the customer rates it 4/5, that's worth investigating.

How it changed the work

Standardisation

Before this system, "doing field research" meant different things in different tribes. Now every CX researcher in the bank uses the same protocol, the same taxonomy and the same definition of a complete interview card.

Speed of insight

The dashboard refreshes the moment a card is saved. Leadership can pull live numbers without waiting for a researcher to "do the analysis." That alone collapsed the loop from a month to live.

Cross-tribe visibility

For the first time, we can compare friction patterns across Kredit, Kartlar and Əmanət side by side. We can see whether "Exposed and Unaware" rates differ by tribe, by branch or by demographic. Insight that lived inside one tribe is now legible across the bank.

Onboarding time for new CJEs

A new researcher can read the rules, study the worked example, and ship their first valid card within 15 minutes. The methodology is encoded in the tool itself rather than living in a Notion doc nobody reads.

Architecture and stack

  • Frontend: single-file HTML + vanilla JavaScript, no build step. Works in any browser, no install.
  • Backend: Google Sheets via Apps Script Web App (REST-like POST/GET). Retry-with-backoff for resilience.
  • State: local cache in localStorage for settings, central truth in Sheet for cards.
  • Filters: client-side filter engine over the cached card array; sub-100ms even at thousands of rows.
  • Dashboard: auto-recomputed counts, percentages, friction themes (word-frequency over free-text fields) and an insight summary that flags outlier segments.

What I owned

End-to-end: research methodology design, taxonomy design, UX and interaction design, all frontend implementation, Apps Script backend, deployment to the CJE community, training materials, and ongoing iteration based on field feedback. No external vendor, no co-designer. A to Z.

Behaviour-Driven Campaign Engine for a Leading Fintech

Customer Insight + CX Strategy · 2025

+26%Conversion rate
+6.4ppCampaign CSAT
−18%Irrelevant complaints
−45%Insight cycle time

Background

The fintech had strong product adoption but engagement and satisfaction were not scaling with it. CSAT had dropped 4pp, complaints about "irrelevant offers" were up 12%, NPS verbatims kept flagging "push overload", and campaign conversion was flat for mass and low-frequency segments.

What I owned

I personally led end-to-end insight discovery, root-cause analysis, behaviour modelling, and the full campaign logic design : behavioural scoring rules, persona segmentation, trigger architecture, message contextualisation rules and dashboard specs. Engineering and ML supported automation; the insight architecture, RCA, segmentation and campaign logic were fully under my ownership.

Problem statement

Campaigns underperformed because they did not reflect real transaction behaviour, timing windows, or contextual triggers. We needed to uncover why customers disengage, how behaviour correlates with CX metrics, which triggers signal interest vs. disinterest, and how insights could be automated and scaled.

Methodology

A. CX metric deep-dive (monthly reviews)

Monthly monitoring across CSAT breakdown by channel and journey, complaints clustering (LLM + human validation), NPS sentiment themes and contact-rate to journey-friction correlations. Surfaced consistent issues: timing mismatch, irrelevant segment targeting, and trigger fatigue.

B. Root cause analysis

RCA using 5 Whys, fishbone diagrams and segmented journey mapping. Three root causes emerged: (1) campaign timing did not match behavioural habits, (2) one-size-fits-all targeting ignored spending context, and (3) high trigger density was driving negative sentiment.

C. Multi-source insight integration

Built a unified view combining transaction logs (MCC, recency, frequency, time windows), in-app behaviour analytics, complaints + CSAT + NPS, customer support chat trends and social sentiment around campaign relevance.

D. Insight automation

Wrote specs for automated dashboards: behaviour scoring, journey friction heatmaps, trigger success/failure diagnostics, persona funnels and CX metric correlation layers. LLM-based clustering reduced analysis time by 45%, with human interpretation as the final validation layer.

Technical flow

Transaction Event
      ↓
Behaviour Scoring (frequency, MCC, time-of-day, anomalies)
      ↓
Persona / Segment Match
      ↓
Trigger Check (context and eligibility)
      ↓
Message Template Selection
      ↓
Delivery (push / in-app)
      ↓
Feedback Loop (conversion, CSAT, complaints)

The campaign engine

Behaviour personas (transaction-based)

Night-time digital shoppers · weekend leisure users · high-frequency digital spenders · travel spenders · health and wellness users · low-frequency "early churn risk" users.

Contextual triggers

Time-of-day behaviour (e.g., 22:00 to 00:00 digital-spend spike), repeated MCC category interest, inactivity-gap churn detection, location-based merchant clusters, and disinterest signals (opt-outs, dismiss patterns).

Personalised messaging framework

Each message aligned to recent transaction context, persona motivation, emotional triggers, pain points surfaced from CX metrics, and preferred communication windows.

Results (8 weeks post-MVP)

  • Conversion rate: +26%
  • Irrelevant-offer complaints: −18%
  • Campaign-linked CSAT: +6.4pp
  • Insight analysis time: −45% (via automation)
  • Low-frequency user retention: +11%
  • High-value segment activation: +21%

Risks and limitations

Used only privacy-safe aggregated data to avoid over-granularity. Kept personas minimalistic to preserve statistical power. Built cold-start fallback scoring using onboarding signals and first few transactions. Set frequency caps and contextual suppression rules to prevent push burnout.

Failure and learning

One early test targeted "night-time spenders" with late-evening offers. For around 10% of users this caused push fatigue and CSAT dipped slightly. We added quiet-hour suppression, treated fatigue indicators as exclusion rules, shifted from fixed time triggers to behaviour-predicted windows, and reviewed early warning signals daily.

Reducing Salary Churn with Behaviour-Based Cashback Packs

Retention Analytics · 2025

−16%Churn reduction
+24%On-us transactions
+11%Wallet share
+12%LTV

Background

A large segment of salary customers showed functional churn: salary arrived monthly, 70 to 80% was transferred to external banks within 24 to 48 hours, on-us card activity stayed extremely low, and many effectively churned within 2 to 3 cycles. This weakened LTV, active usage metrics, cross-product adoption and revenue stability.

Goal: reduce churn by introducing behaviour-personalised cashback packs designed to retain salary funds and grow wallet share.

My role

I led the analytical framework, behavioural segmentation and cashback-pack design : churn definition and behavioural logic, segmentation criteria, rule-based propensity scoring, KPI structure, uplift logic and experiment framework, RCA across transactions + CX + complaints, and stakeholder communication across Product, Data, CX, Operations and Leadership. Product supported commercial decisions; Data Engineering implemented pipelines from the analytical logic I defined.

Behaviour-based churn definition

A customer was flagged as churn-risk if:

  • No activity for 90 days, OR
  • 80% of salary transferred externally within 48 hours for 3 consecutive months

This captured true disengagement, not passive inactivity.

Analytical logic

For each customer and salary month:
    Identify salary credit timestamp
    Sum total salary amount
    Sum external transfers
    outflow_ratio = external_transfers / salary_amount
    hours_to_outflow = first_external_transfer - salary_credit_time
    inactivity_days = days_since_last_on_us_transaction
    Analyse MCC distribution for category behaviours

Data Engineering translated this into production SQL and optimised performance.

Behavioural metrics

Outflow ratio · hours-to-outflow · salary consistency · category (MCC) concentration · inactivity days · external ecosystem dependency · trend shifts in spending. These fed the segmentation and propensity inputs.

Propensity and prioritisation

Designed a lightweight, rule-based propensity scoring model for prioritisation : ranking logic, logistic-inspired weights, and transparent thresholds. Inputs: outflow ratio, hours-to-outflow, inactivity, category-diversity drop, salary pattern stability, share of spend outside ecosystem.

Root-cause drivers

Competitors offered broader cashback ecosystems · existing offers lacked personalisation · habit inertia (salary → external bank → familiar card) · complex selection UX · fee perception pushing customers to alternatives.

Strategic frameworks applied

  • AARRR (retention focus): activation via pack selection, retention via behaviour-relevant incentives, revenue via on-us interchange, referral via lower complaints.
  • BJ Fogg: motivation = reward · ability = simplified flow · trigger = behaviour-timed nudges.
  • JTBD: "When my salary arrives, help me spend it in the most rewarding and convenient ecosystem."

Behavioural segmentation

High External Outflow Customers · Low-Engagement Salary Customers · Partially Engaged Multi-Bank Users · Highly Retained Users.

Solution : personalised cashback packs

Modular bundles aligned with behavioural needs: Groceries and Supermarkets · Online Shopping and Subscriptions · Transport and Ride-Hailing · Health and Wellness · Travel and Events.

Targeting examples: high outflow + grocery-heavy → Grocery Pack; low engagement + external ecommerce → Online Pack; health-driven → Wellness Pack; mixed → Hybrid multi-category.

Experiment design

Test = personalised cashback; control = generic communication. KPIs: churn · outflow ratio · on-us transaction count · salary retained after 7 and 30 days · CSAT + complaints. Measured baseline vs. uplift methodology.

Results (3 months)

  • Churn reduction: 12 to 16%
  • External outflow improvement: 9 to 12 p.p.
  • On-us transaction lift: +18 to +24%
  • CSAT improvement: +5 to +6 p.p.
  • Wallet share uplift: +7 to +11%

Commercial impact

LTV +9 to +12% through higher on-us spend, more interchange revenue and complementary product uptake. Retention lowered effective CAC by 18 to 20%. Cashback cost was 0.7 to 1.1% of incremental revenue; payback improved 25 to 30%; project remained margin-positive.

Risks and mitigation

Incentive dependency → time-boxing and tapering. Adverse selection → ROI filters. Cold-start users → fallback packs. Trigger fatigue → frequency caps. Data bias → cross-validation.

Failure example and learning

An early version over-notified customers → push fatigue. Fixes: quiet-hour suppression, reduced trigger density, behaviour-predicted timing, daily monitoring. CSAT recovered, uplift stabilised.

ABB WRAPPED 2025

From Customer Truth to Decision Confidence · 2025

785KLaunch-day visits
3% → 8%Push open rate
2M+Organic social reach
300KHistorical baseline

Objective

Test whether insight-led framing (patterns, intent, progress) could improve the quality of engagement beyond what annual novelty, timing, and brand strength already delivered.

Context

ABB had access to rich behavioural and transactional data, yet customer engagement was historically driven by promotional mechanics rather than insight-led self-reflection.

Observed outcomes

  • 785,000 launch-day visits (vs. around 300,000 historical peak days)
  • Push open rate increased from around 3% long-term baseline to 8%
  • 2M+ organic social media reach

These were treated as decision-relevant directional signals, not as isolated causal proof.

Role and scope

Customer Insight Analyst : end-to-end insight ownership. I owned insight problem framing, analytical logic and guardrails, and translation of customer data into decision-ready narratives. Hands-on with SQL across multi-million-row behavioural and transactional datasets, partnering with Data Engineering for scale and performance. This was an insight-led IC role focused on framing, interpretation and decision confidence, not a growth-experimentation or heavy-modeling ownership role.

Insight framing : core hypothesis

"If customers recognize patterns, intent, and progress in their data rather than raw spend, engagement becomes more meaningful and durable."

This grounded "customer truth" in observable behavioural signals, keeping insight discussions analytically defensible while remaining interpretable for Product, Marketing and Brand stakeholders.

Data, analytics and validation

Primary inputs: behavioural usage data (frequency, depth, feature interaction); transactional patterns (categories, temporal behaviour); derived constructs (activity intensity, engagement trajectories).

Hands-on analytical work: SQL aggregation across large-scale datasets; definition of time windows, normalization logic and thresholds; sensitivity testing to avoid overfitting small segments; negative-case analysis to identify where narratives failed.

Validation guardrails: temporal consistency across multiple periods; minimum signal strength requirements; explicit discard of unstable or non-interpretable hypotheses. Several early hypotheses were removed after failing these checks.

Advanced ML, predictive scoring and formal causal inference were intentionally not applied in this iteration, due to customer-facing explainability needs, time-to-market constraints, and governance considerations in a financial context. These were documented trade-offs, not capability gaps.

Qualitative signals and customer interpretation

This iteration relied primarily on behavioural data, but qualitative signals informed interpretation: prior CX research on sensitivity to judgment in financial messaging; historical feedback reacting negatively to "you spent more / less" narratives; post-launch sentiment where users echoed insight language ("patterns," "habits," "this felt accurate").

One early insight draft implying "low activity = stagnation" was removed following internal CX review due to emotional risk : a decision later supported by post-launch sentiment.

Counterfactual reasoning and impact interpretation

We explicitly asked: "What would remain if insight framing were removed and only the annual summary format stayed?"

Historical Wrapped-style launches and comparable peak campaigns showed similar timing/brand effects, lower push engagement (around 3% open rate), and more passive consumption.

In this iteration: push messaging shifted from urgency/novelty to self-recognition; generic summaries were replaced with behavioural interpretation; entry intent shifted from "see my stats" to "understand my patterns." These deltas explain why uplift was attributed to insight framing rather than timing alone, while avoiding overclaiming strict causality.

Failure and course correction

A clear misjudgment: I initially overestimated customer appetite for peer comparison. Behavioural data suggested interest, but early narrative testing and CX review revealed discomfort and defensiveness. Comparative insights were scaled back; framing shifted fully to self-referenced progress. This reduced analytical richness but increased acceptance and trust.

Ethics, trust and governance

Some analytically valid insights were excluded or reframed due to risk of negative self-perception, misinterpretation without context, and financial-domain trust sensitivity. These decisions reduced analytical sharpness but protected long-term trust : a deliberate senior-level trade-off.

Organizational lifecycle (beyond launch)

Insight principles were reused in personalisation discussions. "Explainable insight first" became a shared Product and Marketing reference. Wrapped learnings informed how future insight surfaces were framed. The output influenced how insights were used, not only what was delivered.

Scope boundaries (deliberate, not missing)

This case intentionally did not include formal A/B experimentation, numerical uplift attribution or causal effect sizing, or ML-based / advanced causal modeling showcases. At this stage the objective was to validate whether insight-led framing could change customer interpretation and engagement quality in a trust-sensitive environment, not to optimize performance metrics through experimentation. These are identified as next-step layers once framing value is established.

What I would do differently next time

  • Add controlled A/B testing on framing variants
  • Introduce early-stage qualitative validation
  • Separate format uplift from insight uplift more explicitly
  • Attach clearer post-insight action paths

Ganja Mall Website Redesign and CX Optimization

Digital Journey + Measurement · 2024 to 2025

+12 → +31NPS
3.4 → 4.6CSAT (/5)
47s → 18sTime-to-find
+230%EN-version usage

Project overview

Ganja Mall serves a large local population and an increasing number of international visitors arriving through Ganja International Airport. The previous website suffered from usability issues, deep navigation, outdated UI and weak English support. Goal: redesign to improve usability, enhance discoverability, support tourists and lift NPS, CSAT and CES.

Research phase (4 weeks)

Participants (32 total): 22 local users · 6 tourists (Turkish, Kazakh, Arab) · 4 store tenants.

Methods: in-depth interviews (n=18) · heuristic evaluation (Nielsen + mobile-first) · GA4 behavioural analysis · Hotjar heatmaps and scrollmaps · Useberry task tests · time-to-find benchmarking · click-depth analysis.

Key problems identified

  • Average click depth: 4.2
  • 62% of mobile users exited before reaching store info
  • Events page bounce rate: 54%
  • English version missing key content
  • Parking and cinema info hidden
  • No store filters
  • Outdated visual hierarchy

Customer journey mapping

Local users: deep navigation, hard-to-find store list and cinema schedule, visual clutter, no quick-access menu. Tourist users: incomplete English, no clear directions, confusing layout, missing high-intent info (parking, hours, events).

Redesign strategy (8 weeks)

Core principles: mobile-first · reduce friction · improve information architecture · simpler navigation · dual-language structure · tourism-friendly UI.

Key enhancements: clear 3-level navigation · persistent search bar · "Quick Access" panel (Stores, Events, Cinema, Parking) · filterable store directory · clean modern UI aligned with PASHA Malls · complete English version · route and direction page for visitors.

Focus group and validation

12 participants (8 local, 4 tourists). Tools: Figma prototype, Maze tasks, Hotjar test recording. Tasks: find a store via filters · switch language · check cinema schedule · find parking · navigate homepage. Improvements: larger CTAs · sticky EN/AZ switch · simplified filters · persistent search bar · better iconography.

Survey placement and behavioural triggers

Mobile-first surveys on key pages with behaviour-based triggers:

  • CSAT (5-star) on Store Directory, Events, Cinema. Triggers: 50% scroll · mobile exit intent (back button).
  • NPS (0 to 10) on Events, Cinema, second visit. Triggers: 8 to 12 seconds after engagement · scroll depth ≥ 60% · repeat visitor within 48 hours.
  • CES (1 to 7) after task completion. Triggers: store filtering done · cinema schedule viewed · parking page reached · successful language switch.

Statistical validity : Cochran's Formula

Used Cochran's Sample Size Formula (standard for quantitative CX research):

n = 1.96² × 0.5(1−0.5) / 0.05²  ≈  385

Minimum required: 385. Actual responses collected (8 weeks): NPS 612 · CSAT 498 · CES 310 · total 1,420 (3.6× the requirement). Strong statistical validity and reliable comparison.

Business outcomes

The new website became significantly more intuitive and mobile-friendly, improved accessibility for tourists, reduced friction for high-intent tasks, increased content discoverability, strengthened customer satisfaction and validated improvements with statistically significant data.

Leyli AI : Azerbaijan's First AI Mall Guide

Behavioural Research + Activation · 2024 to 2025

2 → 400+Daily questions
100×+Adoption lift
150+Languages supported
0 → #1Info touchpoint

Context

Crescent Mall opened in 2024 as one of the most significant commercial projects in Azerbaijan, positioned as a flagship destination within the PASHA Malls portfolio. Alongside major international tenants (the largest Zara in the Caucasus, one of the country's biggest Mango stores), the mall introduced Leyli AI : the first AI-powered mall guide in Azerbaijan. Despite its novelty and multilingual capacity (150+ languages), Leyli had almost no organic adoption in the first weeks.

The insight challenge

Initial team hypotheses framed it as a marketing gap : that visitors simply did not know Leyli existed. But raw observation suggested otherwise: visitors noticed Leyli, even approached it, yet did not engage. This behavioural conflict pointed to a latent friction point rather than a visibility problem.

My task: diagnose the underlying behavioural barriers preventing adoption of a novel AI experience in a culturally unfamiliar context.

Research approach

a) Behavioural observation (6 hours, non-intrusive)

Watching real visitors revealed: users hesitated to speak aloud in a public space · voice interaction felt "exposed" and uncomfortable · the microphone icon was not cognitively salient · users expected touch-first, not voice-first · visitors paused, looked confused, then walked away. Classic high-friction initiation barriers common in culturally new technologies.

b) Customer Journey Mapping

Two critical drop-off moments: awareness stage : users noticed the device but had no mental model of "AI mall guide → ask me anything"; and action stage : after approaching, users lacked confidence, instruction and clarity on how interaction begins. The problem was not visibility, but actionability.

c) Vendor log review

Daily logs from the Turkish development vendor highlighted extremely low session counts, high incomplete interactions (no microphone activation), a robotic answer tone that did not encourage further engagement, and content misalignment with local communication preferences. Confirmed experience fatigue, not functional failure.

Core insight (root-cause diagnosis)

Usage was blocked by cognitive and cultural friction, not lack of interest.

  1. Psychological friction: speaking out loud in a public setting felt intrusive and socially uncomfortable.
  2. Cognitive friction: the UI did not clearly communicate how to start; it assumed habits typical of more tech-accustomed markets.
  3. Behavioural friction: users were unsure whether they were "allowed" to speak directly to the device and feared being recorded.

This shifted strategy from "market it more" to "redesign the behavioural entry point."

Strategic interventions

a) UX redesign based on behavioural triggers

Enlarged the microphone icon for perceptual salience · added microcopy with explicit instructional cues ("Tap to ask your question") · added a reassurance layer ("Your voice is not stored") · simplified the interaction funnel. Directly reduced cognitive load and increased psychological safety.

b) Tone recalibration

Adjusted Leyli's answer style from formal to conversational, static to human, robotic to contextually playful. Goal: transform Leyli from a tool into a social interaction object.

c) Social activation (TikTok-led)

Reframed the marketing narrative from "AI guide available in Crescent Mall" to "Come try asking Leyli something unexpected." Tapped into curiosity rather than information needs. TikTok storyline showing visitors asking Leyli humorous, human questions created social proof, lowered the social barrier and increased experimentation. This drove the first large wave of adoption. View sample video →

d) Continuous insight loop

Daily Excel log analysis of question types identified recurring needs, new navigation pain points, content gaps and emergent behaviours. These insights informed both Leyli's response updates and the mall's signage and communication.

Outcomes and impact

BeforeAfter (Phase 1)After (Full Optimization)
2 to 3 daily questions50 to 60 daily questions300 to 400+ daily questions

Qualitative impact: Leyli became the mall's most used information touchpoint, gained cultural relevance and recognition among youth, behavioural friction significantly decreased, and the mall strengthened its innovation positioning nationwide.

Strategic takeaway

Technology adoption is not driven by innovation alone. It is driven by human behaviour, psychological safety and cultural context.

The turning point was understanding that the problem was not awareness : it was behavioural entry friction. Solving it required reframing the experience, aligning interaction with cultural norms, reducing cognitive effort, pairing UX with emotionally resonant communication, and reinforcing behaviour through social proof.

TISA Website Transformation

UX Research + IA Redesign · 2019 to 2024

−70%Repetitive inquiries
95%Application completion
+40%Admissions discovery
+21%Mobile engagement

Project overview

TISA is a leading International Baccalaureate (IB) school with a diverse parent base : from young families to international staff and grandparents who often manage the enrollment process. Despite academic excellence, the previous website created friction during the Admissions journey, leaving parents lost, overwhelmed and dependent on the admissions team.

For 12 months I led the Customer Insight and Experience Strategy : uncovering pain points, mapping emotional behaviour, and redesigning the digital journey into something intuitive, clear and accessible for all age groups.

The challenge

  • Parents could not find Admissions or Fees
  • Navigation felt inconsistent and overwhelming
  • Grandparents (60+) struggled significantly
  • Academic pages had too much dense content
  • Mobile experience was not optimised
  • Admissions team received repetitive DMs every day

Goal: design a digital experience that is simple, predictable, and easy for every age group.

Research approach : mixed-method insight framework

Qualitative methods

User interviews · usability testing · contextual inquiry · diary studies · field studies and ethnography · focus groups · card sorting · tree testing · think-aloud protocol · heuristic evaluation. We also ran a final cross-age focus group before production.

Quantitative methods

Click-depth metrics · time-to-find analysis · drop-off mapping · Maze A/B testing · lookback eye-tracking · Hotjar and Smartlook heatmaps · mobile-first analytics.

Before redesign : CJM for the grandparent persona

Key insights

  • Admissions must be immediately visible
  • Older adults scan top-right first
  • Parents need clarity, not depth
  • IB content must be simplified
  • Mobile-first rethinking was essential
  • Internal teams were misaligned, insight unified directions

The solution : new IA and experience

Redefined Information Architecture:

  1. About Us
  2. Learning
  3. Student Life
  4. Community
  5. Admissions (hero journey)
  6. Contact Us

Admissions became a step-by-step guided flow: Inquiry → Application → Documentation → Confirmation.

Prototyping and validation

Eye-tracking showed exact scanning patterns for older vs. younger users. Maze A/B tests validated CTA positions, menu labels and page density. Cross-segment testing with parents, grandparents, students and academic staff measured task success, errors, mobile behaviour and emotional hesitation.

Final outcomes

Quantitative impact

  • −70% repetitive questions (Instagram/WhatsApp)
  • 95% application completion
  • 40% faster Admissions discovery
  • +21% mobile engagement
  • Significant increase in CTA clicks

Qualitative impact

Parents: "Finally clear." · Grandparents: "I can do this alone." · Admissions team: "Support load dropped massively."

My role

As Customer Insight Lead I was responsible for designing the full insight framework · conducting interviews, focus groups and emotional mapping · building journey maps and synthesising pain points · leading IA redesign and content clarity strategy · working with the UK development team · running all validation cycles · aligning academic departments through data · and ensuring every decision was insight-backed.

Reflection

This project showed how deep insight + behavioural understanding can transform a complex, multi-stakeholder digital journey. By focusing on clarity, emotional ease and inclusive experience design, we delivered a website that finally works for every parent : from young families to grandparents.

Improving Online Conversion for a Global FMCG Brand

Funnel Diagnosis on a Leading E-Commerce Marketplace

↑Conversion rate
↓Cart abandonment
↑Basket size
↓Negative reviews

Background

A global FMCG brand collaborated with a leading e-commerce marketplace to improve product performance across several categories. Despite high visibility, conversion rate and overall user flow did not meet expectations. My role: analyse behavioural data, detect friction points and recommend clear, realistic improvements for marketing, product and trade teams.

Key challenges identified

  • High Add-to-Cart → Checkout drop-off
  • Lower conversion on mobile compared to desktop
  • Users browsing mostly in the evening but purchasing in the morning
  • Limited visibility into frequently bought-together items
  • Variant visibility issues on mobile
  • Stock-outs leading to rating drops

Methodology

A) Funnel and checkout friction analysis

Three simple, reliable metrics: Step Drop % (users dropping between checkout steps) · Time-to-Checkout (add-to-cart to payment screen) · Payment Click Rate (% clicking "Proceed to Payment").

Recommendations after identifying friction:

  1. Move the "Proceed to Checkout" button to a more visible position on mobile.
  2. Reduce checkout from 3 steps to 2.
  3. Show variant selection earlier, so users do not reach checkout with missing options.
  4. Simplify delivery and payment information to reduce cognitive load.

B) Timing behaviour analysis

Timestamp data revealed high browsing in the late evening but higher conversions during morning hours : a timing mismatch.

C) Basket analysis

Simple frequency-based method: extracted all products appearing in the same basket, counted repeating pairs across multiple weeks, grouped combinations by category.

Threshold: a product pair was considered meaningful if it repeated at least 3 weeks in a row, or consistently across different user segments. This ensured patterns reflected real behaviour, not campaign-driven spikes. Common bundles: cleaning combos, personal care sets, baby essentials.

D) Review and rating analysis

Reviewed low ratings to detect recurring issues: packaging · delivery delays · stock-outs.

E) Device performance analysis

To understand mobile frustrations: scroll depth (did users reach variant options?) · event counts (taps on size/pack/colour selectors) · heatmap visibility (were variants on screen?) · variant click visibility rate (users who saw but did not interact).

Finding: variant selectors were often positioned below the fold, causing hesitation and abandonment.

Stakeholder management

Weekly insight summaries · decision-focused performance dashboard · clear, action-oriented category recommendations shared with Marketing, Product, Trade and Category managers.

KPI framework

Primary: conversion rate · cart abandonment rate · average basket size. Secondary: product page engagement (variant clicks, scroll depth) · mobile vs. desktop conversion gap · review sentiment distribution.

Key insights

  1. Significant friction before payment step.
  2. Evening browsing did not convert immediately : timing mismatch.
  3. Strong basket repetition patterns → bundle opportunity.
  4. Variant visibility issues on mobile lowered CR.
  5. Stock-outs affected both ratings and customer trust.

Recommendation prioritisation (effort vs. impact)

  • High impact, low effort → implement immediately
  • Medium effort, high impact → short-term roadmap
  • High effort, medium impact → longer-term enhancements

Final recommendations

  • Highlight bundle opportunities directly on PDP
  • Schedule campaigns during morning (high-conversion) hours
  • Move variant options above the fold on mobile
  • Simplify mobile CTAs
  • Improve stock monitoring and review alerts

Impact

Without disclosing confidential numbers: conversion improved consistently · cart abandonment decreased · basket sizes increased for visible bundles · negative reviews reduced · teams gained a structured insight process they continued using.

Tools used

SQL · Excel and Sheets · Marketplace analytics · Tableau.
